slides.title: Greedy Best-First Search (GBFS)
slides.content: Greedy Best-First Search (GBFS) • Strategy: expand a node that you think is closest to a goal state • Heuristic: estimate of distance to nearest goal for each state • A common case: • Greedy best-first takes you straight to a goal • Worst-case: like a badly-guided DFS … b … b

slides.title: Beam Search
slides.content: Beam Search Variant of breadth-first search and greedy best-first • just like Breadth-first search: expand all nodes that are at the same depth, but after every level: only keep the k best paths on the frontier, remove all others • just like Greedy: choose which k paths to keep based on their heuristic value

slides.title: Beam Search Properties, beam size k
slides.content: Beam Search Properties, beam size k How much space does the frontier take? Queue has always size k, but expansion requires size O(kb) What nodes does BFS expand? If a solution is found: O(skb) otherwise: O(mkb) Is it complete? NO! you may throw away a needed path Is it optimal? NO!  ‘(greedy) hill-climbing search’: K = 1 (stick to 1 path, no ‘backtracking’) … b 1 node b nodes b2 nodes bm nodes s tiers bs nodes

slides.title: Combining UCS and Greedy
slides.content: Combining UCS and Greedy Uniform-cost orders by path cost, or backward cost g(n) Greedy orders by goal proximity, or forward cost h(n) A* Search orders by the sum: f(n) = g(n) + h(n) S a d b G h=5 h=6 h=2 1 8 1 1 2 h=6 h=0 c h=7 3 e h=1 1 Example: Teg Grenager S a b c e d d G G g = 0 h=6 g = 1 h=5 g = 2 h=6 g = 3 h=7 g = 4 h=2 g = 6 h=0 g = 9 h=1 g = 10 h=2 g = 12 h=0

slides.title: A*: the core idea
slides.content: A*: the core idea Expand a node n most likely to be on an optimal path Expand a node n with lowest value of g(n) + h*(n)  g(n) is the cost from root to n  h*(n) is the optimal cost from n to the closest goal We seldom know h*(n) but might have a heuristic approximation h(n) A* = tree search with priority queue ordered by f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

slides.title: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking
slides.content: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking Proof: Imagine suboptimal B is on the frontier Some ancestor n of A is on the frontier, too (maybe A itself!) Claim: n will be expanded before B 1. f(n) ≤ f(A) f(n) = g(n) + h(n) Definition of f-cost g(n) + h(n) ≤ g(n) + h*(n) Admissibility of h … g(A) = f(A) h = 0 at a goal A B n f(n) ≤ g(A) (rewrite)

slides.title: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking
slides.content: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking Proof: Imagine B is on the frontier Some ancestor n of A is on the frontier, too (maybe A itself!) Claim: n will be expanded before B 1. f(n) ≤ f(A) 2. f(A) < f(B) … A B n g(A) < g(B) Suboptimality of B f(A) < f(B) h = 0 at a goal

slides.title: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking
slides.content: Optimality of A* Tree Search: Blocking Proof: Imagine B is on the frontier Some ancestor n of A is on the frontier, too (maybe A itself!) Claim: n will be expanded before B 1. f(n) ≤ f(A) 2. f(A) < f(B) 3. n is expanded before B All ancestors of A are expanded before B A is expanded before B A* tree search is optimal … A B n f(n) ≤ f(A) < f(B)

slides.title: Creating Admissible Heuristics
slides.content: Creating Admissible Heuristics Often, admissible heuristics are solutions to relaxed problems, where new actions are available Problem P2 is a relaxed version of P1 if A2(s) ⊇ A1(s) for every s Theorem: h2 *(s) ≤ h1 *(s) for every s, so h2 *(s) is admissible for P1 1 5 366

slides.title: Alternative: Consistency of Heuristics
slides.content: Alternative: Consistency of Heuristics Main idea: estimated heuristic costs ≤ actual costs Admissibility: heuristic cost ≤ actual cost to goal h(A) ≤ h*(A) Consistency: heuristic “arc” cost ≤ actual cost for each arc h(A) – h(C) ≤ c(A,C) or h(A) ≤ c(A,C) + h(C) (=triangle inequality) Note: h* necessarily satisfies triangle inequality Consequences of consistency: The f(n) (=g(n)+h(n)) value along a path never decreases: h(A) ≤ c(A,C) + h(C) => g(A) + h(A) ≤ g(A) + c(A,C) + h(C) => g(A) + h(A) ≤ g(AC) + h(C) => f(A) ≤ f(AC) h= 1 A G h= 2 C 1 3 h= 4

slides.title: Optimality of A* Graph Search
slides.content: Optimality of A* Graph Search Sketch: consider what A* does with a consistent heuristic: Fact 1: In tree search, A* expands nodes in increasing total f value (f-contours) Fact 2: For every state s, nodes that reach s optimally are expanded before nodes that reach s suboptimally (f value along path never decreases) Result: A* graph search is optimal … f ≤ 3 f ≤ 2 f ≤ 1

slides.title: Optimality
slides.content: Optimality Tree search: A* is optimal if heuristic is admissible Graph search: A* with closed set is optimal if heuristic is consistent Consistency implies admissibility Most natural admissible heuristics tend to be consistent, especially if from relaxed problems

slides.title: Upgrade: optimal A* with admissible heuristic
slides.content: Upgrade: optimal A* with admissible heuristic S (0+2) A (1+4) B (1+1) C (2+1) G (5+0) C (3+1) G (6+0) Search tree Not expanded due to loop breaking: C already in ‘closed’ set Closed set stores which states expanded Closed dictionary ‘closed_cost’ stores which state AND at what cost expanded New check: expand if state s not in closed dictionary OR if current-cost g(n) < closed_cost[s] Then update closed_cost dictionary Upside: less restricted when designing heuristics Downside: A crappy heuristic might make us expand the same state many times… g(n) ?< closed_cost[C] Yes: 2 < 3

slides.title: But…
slides.content: But… A* keeps the entire explored region in memory => will run out of space before you get bored waiting for the answer There are variants that use less memory (AIMA Section 3.5.5): IDA* works like iterative deepening, except it uses an f-limit instead of a depth limit On each iteration, remember the smallest f-value that exceeds the current limit, use as new limit Very inefficient when f is real-valued and each node has a unique value RBFS is a recursive depth-first search that uses an f-limit = the f-value of the best alternative path available from any ancestor of the current node When the limit is exceeded, the recursion unwinds but remembers the best reachable f-value on that branch SMA* uses all available memory for the queue, minimizing thrashing When full, drop worst node on the queue but remember its value in the parent

slides.title: A*: Summary
slides.content: A*: Summary A* orders nodes in the queue by f(n) = g(n) + h(n) A* is optimal for trees/graphs with admissible/consistent heuristics Heuristic design is key: often use relaxed problems g g h h
